#602. The US Lost Its Measles Elimination Status. It’ll Take Years to Get It Back

The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: Two more people died from measles, bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and the country officially lost its status as a country that had eliminated the highly infectious disease.

The US eliminated measles in 2000 and maintained that status for 26 years. Now, the nation faces an uphill battle to vanquish the virus once more, and it will take years to be measles-free again.

Noel Brewer, a professor of health behavior at the University of North Carolina, presented a report last week to the Pan American Health Organization showing continuous measles transmission for at least 12 months in the US—erasing one of the nation’s greatest public health achievements.

WIRED asked him how he felt after PAHO officials reached a consensus that the country was no longer measles-free. He paused.

“I have not actually thought about my reaction,” he says. After a beat, he says that the loss is “a somber moment for public health” that’s particularly wrenching because it’s a “completely avoidable situation.” Mexico and Canada have managed to wind down their outbreaks, but “measles in America is a runaway train,” Brewer says. “There's no end in sight, and it may even be gaining speed.”

PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr. officially announced the change in status on Tuesday. “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” he said at a press conference. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.” Bolivia and Mexico also lost their elimination status this year; Canada lost it a year ago.

Brewer presented three key lines of evidence showing that measles has become endemic in the US. The outbreak in Utah and Arizona has gone on for more than 12 months, and the US has had measles cases every week since January 20, 2025. The genomic data also shows a great deal of similarity across states, indicating the clusters are closely linked—and each week, there are cases where the sources can’t be confirmed, indicating they didn’t come from travel or known contact with other patients.

“We have a problem on our hands,” says William Moss, epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins. And it’s not going away anytime soon. To reclaim its status as measles-free, the US will have to prove it has gone a full year without continued transmission. That’s unlikely to happen under the Trump administration—and its actions have made it more difficult for future leaders.

“Reestablishing elimination is not just about reporting fewer cases—it also requires convincing the world that we have a strong enough surveillance system to find cases and deaths,” Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University, tells WIRED in a text.

The fact that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments differ on how many people have died from measles “is a sign of dysfunction,” Nuzzo says. There have been 10 confirmed measles deaths so far this year—seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, and one in New York—but the CDC only lists six.

Such chaos also breeds distrust, says Frederic Bertley, president and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry. That's “a huge problem” for a public trying to parse who is telling the truth and whether they should listen, he says.

Even as measles was eliminated, anti-vaccine rhetoric began to rise, especially around the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Vaccination rates began falling—spurred in part by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an environmental lawyer turned anti-vaccine activist who published a now-retracted article alleging a link between vaccines and autism in 2005. He continued crusading against vaccines as head of Children’s Health Defense and at the helm of the Department of Health and Human Services during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration has done little to stop the outbreaks, cutting billions in funding from state, local, territorial, and tribal public health departments and offering conflicting messages on vaccines. During a televised February 2025 cabinet meeting following the first child death in a decade, Kennedy said “it's not unusual, we have measles outbreaks every year.” The CDC hasn’t held a single press conference on measles throughout the entire outbreak; as PAHO was making its measles status announcement on Tuesday, HHS sent out an email about Kennedy’s cooking show.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said in a statement. “Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Kennedy posted on X, “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

To regain its elimination status, the US needs to address barriers to health care access, missed vaccination opportunities, misinformation, and vaccine hesitancy, Barbosa said. That includes mounting wide-reaching vaccination campaigns, expanding laboratory testing capacity, and responding quickly to cases, including contact tracing. It’s the bread and butter of public health, but the longer it takes to create a comprehensive response, the more it will cost, experts warn.

Future efforts to contain measles will require “a stronger centralized federal response to these outbreaks” paired with support for “very local responses,” says Moss. That means identifying communities with long-standing under-vaccination and understanding why, he says, as well as improving trust in public health guidance.

“Immunity gaps” tend to concentrate in specific geographic areas and communities, and national or even state-level data can “mask these significant inequalities, providing an incomplete picture of the population's actual level of protection,” Barbosa said.

The CDC announced $100 million in August and September—more than a year after the outbreak began—to help fund state and regional efforts to combat measles, but Congress will need to allocate $100 million to $400 million more for measles elimination in coming months, Brewer says.

“More than 90 percent of children get the measles vaccine, Brewer points out. “This is a vaccine that has extraordinary public support, and it goes across the aisle.”

But to achieve herd immunity, vaccination rates need to be at least 95 percent due to how contagious the disease is. High transmissibility also means measles is very hard to uproot once it begins to spread.

Yet ending national measles transmission is “its own reward,” Brewer says. It spares children’s lives, keeps them out of hospitals, and prevents blindness and other lifelong complications. “We no longer have that benefit,” he says. “Children are now being stalked by this incurable and deadly disease.”

#601. Germany news: Merz, Söder aim to revisit electricity tax cut

The Christian Democrats are in Munich, pushing to revive some tax relief that didn't make it into the budget after talks last week. And Manuela Schwesig faces a vote on a new term as regional leader. Follow DW.

Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow. Bis dann!

Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.

It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."

Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.

Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.

By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

A group of five EU member states, including Germany, have entered talks over a scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

The plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had first been announced back in September.

Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.

The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car company's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.

The Elon Musk-owned company said construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.

"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle currently stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.

Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.

The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.

The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.

She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).

While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.

"We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz said.

Merz said that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented."

He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany."

Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.

Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad."

After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short."

He said that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households."

Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.

It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.

Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.

Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really important."

He said the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.

"That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement."

Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process."

A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.

Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.

The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.

"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order."

Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.

Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.

The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, said the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.

He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan."

"The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen said.

The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has said that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.

Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.

"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.

She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.

Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.

Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.

Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.

And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.

If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.

Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he said play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.

"I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp said. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started."

A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.

The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.

Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.

A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.

State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.

A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.

The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.

The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.

Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative  Christian Democrats(CDU).

No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.

The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.

It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.

The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.

The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.

But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.

Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.

The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.

Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.

Far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.

And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.

The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.

Stay with us for more on these stories and whatever else develops around Germany on November 16.

#600. A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a new way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

The second state was particularly important because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," says senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity."

A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

Materials provided by The University of Osaka. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into the night sky. Traced by a flashlight beam switched on and off, the dashes and dots of a Morse code message captured in this time exposure from the Emirates Astronomical Observatory, are read V-G-R. That's a call sign for the Voyager 1 spacecraft currently in interstellar space some 26 billion kilometers away. How long did it take the message to reach humanity's most distant interstellar spacecraft? Traveling at the speed of light, the answer is one day. In fact, the Voyager 1 spacecraft was confirmed to reach its one light-day distance milestone on November 18, at 10:16:07 UTC, nearly 50 years after launch in 1977. #598. Feds arrest top official of healthcare company, alleging illegal drug importation

U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.

Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody.

Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant said John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed.

CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the company and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP.

AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have said is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized.

On its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The company said it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand.

But the affidavit said that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States …."

The affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.

The company's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court."

The company has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC.

And in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the company, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor.

In an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris said last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally.

The central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients.

But an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs."

In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV.

In a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson said the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk."

CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.

— CNBC's Paige Tortorelli and Melissa Lee contributed to this report

#597. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#596. An AI Debt Collection Service Exposed 6.6 Million Accounts and 315,000 Call Recordings

Two vulnerabilities in the India-based AI-driven debt collection platform CreditNirvana exposed 6.6 million accounts and about 315,000 call recordings from the company's agentic call center, according to research released on Wednesday. Owned by the Indian fintech company Perfios, the platform is built to “read a borrower’s full context, decide the next best action, and execute it autonomously, continuously, and within policy.”

The bugs were patched in CreditNirvana's systems in June and were disclosed publicly in October. But independent researcher Eaton Zveare, who found and disclosed them, notes that, while the vulnerabilities were active, they exposed personal information on millions of borrowers. Details about financial collections are inherently—perhaps obviously—sensitive, because they relate to unpaid accounts or debts and often involve extensive documentation of people's personal histories.

“They fixed it in one day, which was great, but this is really a pretty significant case,” Zveare tells WIRED. “Some of the largest fintech firms across India use this company to autonomously collect debts, so they naturally hold data, including credit scores, call recordings, transcripts, court records, and other sensitive documents. There’s just so much in there that makes it a very sensitive issue.”

CreditNirvana and Perfios did not return WIRED's requests for comment. Zveare says he worked directly with India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) to get the vulnerabilities fixed. CERT-In categorized one vulnerability as “high” severity and the other as “critical” severity.

The high-severity vulnerability impacted the call center data, exposing hundreds of thousands of calls as well as recommendations for next steps generated by the platform after calls were complete. It could also have been exploited to allow an attacker to manage AI agents within the platform and direct their own agentic campaigns.

The critical severity vulnerability impacted CreditNirvana's main platform, and Zveare says it specifically exposed the data of three corporate customers—all prominent Indian financial services firms—using CreditNirvana for their collections. The data also exposed millions of individuals’ accounts, which contain credit reports, ID cards, case management details, and legal documents, along with certain types of communications, including millions of emails, texts, and call transcripts related to financial services, unpaid accounts, and collections. The vulnerability also could have been exploited by an attacker to track the location of human debt collection agents and for some administrative privileges within the system.

“Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to enumerate platform users, establish sessions as arbitrary users including administrative users, access and modify sensitive information with the privileges of the impersonated user,” CERT-In wrote.

Zveare says he is relieved that the issue was resolved quickly, but is conscious that the bugs were potentially present in CreditNirvana's systems for years. As AI is integrated into more and more automated systems, synthesizing data from a greater number of sources and using it to draw conclusions, Zveare says, the episode serves as “an important example of an AI-powered service having a very sensitive data exposure.”

#595. Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."

But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

#594. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies."

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research

The results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?"

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support."

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

#592. COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels

The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

The goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.

Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."

Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.

"For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.

"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.

Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."

Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.

"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance."

"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," said Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.

"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.

"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," said Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030."

But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."

David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, said the draft text showed a level of "seriousness" on important issues like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.

"The question is whether the level of ambition on those issues is carried through into the final outcome here," said Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days."

Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.

#591. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

#589. A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics

A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors

Previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

The UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

If cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," said Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted."

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

The new approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter

The challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement."

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most important unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

One possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Original written by Michelle Franklin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
