#588. The future of tech will not be inclusive by default

Ten years ago, QueerTech began with a feeling that too many 2SLGBTQI+ people in the technology sector know well: not belonging.

My co-founder Andy Saldaña and I were working at different companies in tech and kept running into the same frustration. We could see the possibility of the sector around us, had the skills to succeed, and believed technology, when stewarded responsibly, could change lives. Yet we could not see a place for ourselves, as queer professionals, within it.

I grew up in Morocco, where being queer was, and continues to be, illegal. In 2007, I left for New York City in pursuit of the "American Dream." There, I quickly realized this dream was based on a contradiction — opportunity without equal rights. Finally, I moved to Montreal, drawn to Canada’s reputation for respecting people across cultures, religions, and identities.

Across this journey, I expected geography to change my sense of belonging. It never did. So in 2016, Andy and I started small. QueerTech was a volunteer-run community group built around a simple need: to find one another, create connections, and make space for queer people in an industry where many of us felt invisible.

Today, QueerTech is a national nonprofit working across workforce development, entrepreneurship, research, responsible technology, and community. Our scale has changed, but the need has not. What has evolved is our understanding of what meaningful inclusion requires: not only creating spaces where queer people belong, but breaking down the systemic barriers that determine who gets access to opportunities, who advances into leadership, and who has the power to shape the future of technology.

The scope of our mission, spanning inclusive technology and professional wellbeing, demands ambitious goals and innovative programming grounded in collaboration and practical impact. Our community-first approach supports 2SLGBTQI+ professionals from industry entry through career advancement and entrepreneurship, while driving systemic change through partnerships with industry, investors, regulators, and community organizations.

QueerTech’s goals for the Canadian tech ecosystem are:

Increasing 2SLGBTQI+ representation to 20 percent across the sector.

Advancing 2SLGBTQI+ leadership representation to 5 percent.

Increasing funding for 2SLGBTQI+-owned ventures to 15 percent of total invested capital.

QT Access: Building pathways into tech through skills development, mentorship and career preparation.

QT Leaders: Advancing professionals into decision-making roles that shape workplace culture, policy and innovation.

QT Founders: Equipping queer entrepreneurs with tools, networks and access to capital.

QT Events: Creating safer spaces for connection, learning and opportunity, both in-person and online.

Our responsible technology priorities center on the QT Inclusive AI Initiative. Launched in 2026, it combines self-assessment tools, inclusive AI training, national research, community dialogue, practical governance frameworks and cross-sector partnerships to strengthen AI literacy, accountability, inclusive practices, and collaboration.

These efforts are grounded in a growing body of evidence about the barriers 2SLGBTQI+ professionals face, both within the technology sector and through the systems it creates. QueerTech’s 2026 research makes the scale of those challenges difficult to ignore.

QueerTech’s national Industry Census found 2SLGBTQI+ tech workers reported harassment and discrimination at roughly twice the rate of their non-2SLGBTQI+ peers: 44 percent reported harassment and 50 percent discrimination. Another 35 percent reported bias from AI hiring tools (versus 22 percent of peers). The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Inclusion in technology can no longer be measured only by who works inside the industry. We must also examine the systems the industry builds and deploys, including who participates in decisions, whose perspectives influence innovation, and who benefits from these advanced technologies.

This year, QueerTech studied both sides of that equation. Our research into AI development found 43 percent of Canadian technology companies reported limited to no formal processes for addressing bias, while 71 percent reported limited to no organizational support for equitable representation.

Our research into AI use in human resources also exposed a significant disconnect between institutional perceptions and queer professionals’ experiences. While 86 percent of HR professionals believed 2SLGBTQI+ employees were "comfortable being out," our 2026 Census found only 37 percent of queer professionals were "out" at work to a great extent — a disparity of nearly 50 percent.

The cost of that disconnect is higher than any one workplace. When queer professionals are overlooked, stalled or pushed out, companies lose skill, experience, and perspective. When people most likely to encounter bias are missing from product decisions, preventable blind spots can become features of automated systems and travel farther, faster and with less visibility.

That is not just an inclusion problem. It is a talent, product, and competitiveness problem for Canada’s innovation economy. As Canada invests in its technological future and digital sovereignty, we cannot afford to overlook talent, limit leadership access, or build technologies that fail to serve the people who depend on them.

The next question is what the sector does with that evidence.

On Nov. 18 and 19, more than 700 tech professionals will gather in Toronto for the 2026 QT Qonference (QTQ) under the theme Who Gets to Trust AI? This question is critical, given that trust in technology is shaped by various decentralized, and often competing, entities across the entire ecosystem. Developers build the systems. Employers decide how they are used. Executives set priorities. Policymakers create the rules. Workers and communities experience the results.

QTQ convenes these groups to address the same challenges from different perspectives. Better decisions happen when the people building, governing, and using technology are at the same table, but participation alone is not enough. Meaningful change requires institutions to translate conversation into action: removing barriers to opportunity, embedding accountability into technology development and deployment, and giving affected communities a meaningful role in shaping these technologies.

The future of tech will not be inclusive by default. It will be shaped by who is included in the decisions that define it. The responsibility belongs to all of us — industry leaders, investors, policymakers, and communities — to ensure that innovation expands opportunity rather than reinforces existing inequalities. Inclusion is not a concession to innovation; it’s a condition for responsible, sustainable innovation.

This article represents the opinion of its writer.

QueerTech is a national nonprofit advancing 2SLGBTQI+ talent, entrepreneurship, and inclusive technology across Canada’s tech ecosystem. Through community-led programming, original research, strategic partnerships, and actionable inclusion tools, QueerTech builds pathways to opportunity for queer professionals, leaders, and entrepreneurs while working with ecosystem partners to address the institutional barriers that limit access, advancement, and participation. Guided by its Vision 2034, QueerTech is working toward a technology ecosystem where queer people don't just participate — they thrive, lead, and help shape the future of innovation.

#587. The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?

The Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has become a focal point for the far right. Many of its members and staff have ties to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations.

The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."

The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."

Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

This article was originally written in German.

#586. Scout Motors has 212,000 vehicle reservations as $2 billion South Carolina plant nears completion

BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the company nears completion of its new $2 billion plant here, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC.

The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed company's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.

Reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases.

Keogh said he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more important thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears.

"It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh said during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell."

Keogh said achieving an order book of 12 to 18 months "would be great" and is something he thinks the company can do before production. Scout on Thursday said plant construction is "in its final phase."

Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, that include an internal combustion engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries.

Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the company to decide to offer EREVs as well.

Keogh said extended-range and SUV models are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs.

The CEO also said the company is drawing interest from its target markets, which include owners of off-road vehicles such as the Ford Bronco and Jeep Wrangler as well as full-size pickup trucks and U.S. EV leader Tesla.

Given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh said the company is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company plans to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models.

Both the Traveler and Terra are expected to start at under $60,000. The EREV models are expected to feature more than 500 miles of range, according to the company, compared with 300 miles of range for the all-electric models.

"The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh said. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through."

His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry.

Keogh said Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed.

Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra, which feature sleek, yet rugged, exteriors that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

#585. The ‘GTA 6’ Work Blackout Is Here

Somewhere out there, right at this moment, a couple is probably still negotiating the final terms of a contract that permits one partner to play Grand Theft Auto VI around the clock for an entire week following its Thursday release. Adults who grew up on the felony-based video game franchise are taking steps to secure sick days—and some, no doubt, are granting their own kids permission to stay home from school (despite warnings from their teachers). Streamers on Twitch and YouTube stand ready to conquer the enhanced and expanded virtual domain of Vice City, seeking out every last Easter egg.

So don’t be surprised if a console owner in your life is curiously unavailable between now and Thanksgiving. The 13-year-wait for this latest installment of the series has felt interminable enough to inspire a meme used in reaction to any surprising or unprecedented news: “We got [fill in the blank] before GTA VI.”

Especially within the tech and gaming industries, the expectation is that many developers won’t be clocking in on Thursday or Friday. (GTA VI officially launches for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S at midnight local time on Thursday, November 19, according to publisher Rockstar Games.)

“I’m not going to question whether folks are really sick on their sick days or how they spend a vacation day,” says Mike, an executive of a gaming studio with more than a thousand employees, who requested a pseudonym to avoid damaging professional relationships within the industry. “I want them to spend time engaging with the medium we love, and there’s no question that playing lots of video games helps you make video games.”

In October, the HR software company BambooHR concluded through data analysis and a survey of salaried workers that the PTO request rate for November 19 is nearly 13 percent higher than equivalent days in past years, while Xbox is running a promotional campaign in which gamers can generate notes from a Dr. Xbox (DJ Khaled in glasses and a lab coat) claiming that they have a “Vitamin G” deficiency and are unable to work.

A few companies are getting ahead of the productivity slump; the hardware and software manufacturer Logitech, for example, announced earlier this month that all 7,000 employees would be granted a paid day off for gaming, to be scheduled any time within a year or so. In announcing the policy, the company cited internal studies on the ways that gaming may potentially improve job performance and mental health.

Riot Games, the publisher behind League of Legends and Valorant, has likewise made arrangements for the blockbuster event. “We have an open PTO policy, and we’ve seen leaders encourage their teams to enjoy the first day of release,” Joe Hixson, Riot Games vice president of communications, tells WIRED. “On our main campus, we'll be celebrating with a special-themed lunch menu and snacks that pay homage to the game. We also expect to see people firing it up in our console rooms during breaks and after hours.”

Riot additionally offers the Play Fund, a stipend of $25 a month for employees to spend on gaming titles across platforms and genres. “It makes us better developers by deepening our understanding of what makes a great player experience,” Hixson says.

Mike tells WIRED that on in-office workdays, the company has a typical absentee rate of 5 to 7 percent due to vacations, illness, travel, and the like. He estimates that on Thursday, it will be more like 10 or 12 percent. “Now, on the Friday, will there be some number of employees who are ‘working’ when they’re at home but also suspiciously slow to answer messages while they have big chunks of their calendar blocked out for ‘deep individual work?’” says the studio leader. “Yeah, probably.”

But it’s hardly unusual in the business for people to select their days off to accommodate a major game release, Mike says. In 2023, he was out for three days to play The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, which he recalls as “paradise.”

That said, he notes that the next leap forward for GTA is no ordinary affair. The hype for this franchise, he explains, “breaks containment,” reaching people who have not bought a new title in years.

That’s why even companies without ties to gaming culture have been making allowances for so-called Grand Theft Auto Flu. On Monday, the social team for the luxury real estate firm Serhant posted a video of CEO Ryan Serhant (also the host of the Netflix reality show Owning Manhattan) agreeing with an employee that if the clip garnered 400,000 likes, the office would close for GTA day. “You’ll never get that,” Serhant predicted.

The post picked up 1.4 million likes within 24 hours, prompting an update on Tuesday: The firm would honor Serhant’s promise. “We are big supporters of our team, their passions both in and out of real estate, and all things culture and tech,” Serhant said in a statement to WIRED, noting that “13 years of anticipation deserves a day off.” The company announced a floating holiday to staff on Wednesday, to be used any time before the end of 2026.

Also on Wednesday, Arizona Beverages announced a sweepstakes for social media followers who may have felt they couldn’t afford to miss a work shift. Dropping a PTO request for GTA day in the comment section, the company said, would enter that person for a chance to win $500 to cover their lost hours.

With this level of fanfare, nearly 16 million preorders bringing in revenue of $1.5 billion, and expectations of 45 million sales in its launch quarter, GTA VI is poised to be the most significant entertainment event of the year and the biggest video game of all time. It’s little wonder, then, that some have warned about the global economy slowing down this week as fans ignore their email inboxes and Slack messages to indulge in some extended role-play as streetwise criminals. One economist has estimated that the GTA release could cost the US economy $1 billion in lost productivity.

Mike isn’t buying this, however, arguing that the hype about “how GTA will impact the GDP or cause a failure of the power grid or whatever are just silly.” He points out that “PC is the biggest individual platform, and the PC launch timing is still unclear.” Neither have Rockstar and Take-Two announced a launch date for the game’s online multiplayer mode; only the single-player experience will be available on Thursday.

Andy Garin, an associate professor of economics at Carnegie Mellon University, also finds the concerns about sluggish market activity to be overblown.

“Speculation about a hit to productivity around these kinds of events pops up a lot, particularly during the Olympics or World Cup, when time zone differences mean major events are during the workday,” Garin says. “I don't think the release date of GTA VI will be that different than these sort of events that happen all the time, particularly if workers are using their allotted PTO or scheduling flexibility baked into their jobs.”

Malcolm Robinson, who has a YouTube channel dedicated to gaming and works at a veterans hospital, tells WIRED that the GTA release just happens to fall on his day off. “I plan on playing it for about eight to 12 hours straight on the first night,” he says.

Others have had no difficulty setting that time aside. One redditor who works as the distribution coordinator for a chain of auto shops in Colorado and requested anonymity out of concern for professional consequences says that he would have called in sick on Thursday but had the option to use PTO. His supervisor asked if it was to play GTA, which he confirmed. “He was like, ‘I get it, enjoy,’” this gamer reports. He plans to play along with his girlfriend, who is also taking the day off, and is excited to “sink my teeth into it before the entire thing gets spoiled.”

James Lord, a data entry coordinator in Edmonton, Alberta, tells WIRED that he initially offered to let his team take Thursday off for GTA purposes. When none of them expressed interest in the game, he says, he “jumped at the opportunity” to claim the day for himself. He’s been playing Grand Theft Auto since the original top-down POV game for the PC came out in the late 1990s.

Lord, too, is wary of spoilers—he locked down his social media on Tuesday night to avoid any—but nostalgia and lifelong relationships are even better reasons to jump into GTA VI as soon as he can. He’s going to boot up the game while on a call with his brother, who lives across the country, and they’ll be joined by friends living in Pennsylvania and Texas. It’s a reunion experience that wouldn’t be possible without a break from the 9-to-5 job.

#583. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#582. What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

#581. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

#579. NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

#578. AOC, Paris Hilton push for House vote on explicit deepfake bill

Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, socialite Paris Hilton, and others called for the House of Representatives to vote on the long-stalled, bipartisan DEFIANCE Act at a Capitol Hill press conference on Tuesday.

DEFIANCE stands for Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits, and the legislation would let survivors sue people who knowingly share, solicit, or receive sexually explicit and nonconsensual deepfakes (AI-generated images or video), according to a press release by anti-sexual violence organization RAINN.

The bill would also establish a 10-year statute of limitations that would begin when the survivor turns 18 or discovers the violation, whichever is later.

#577. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but new research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A New Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle."

#576. Australia’s Plan to Manage Neil the Unruly Seal Involves ‘Hazing’ and ‘Seal Enrichment’

There is a 6-year-old elephant seal in Tasmania named Neil who has a taste for light property damage during the winter months. Now, the state has a management plan.

Neil's annual “hauling out” and subsequent misadventures on the southeastern part of the island has delighted locals, making him a local mascot and a viral social media star.

But Neil’s on-land hijinks—as he experiences his yearly “catastrophic molt,” during which he, like all elephant seals, sheds and replaces his top level of fur and epidermis— has also created headaches for local officials. Neil, who weighs over 2,000 pounds, has destroyed walkways, flattened bollards, bowled through fences, and rammed vehicles. The enormous and growing public interest in Neil has also been a source of concern, as officials spend tens of thousands of Australian dollars to keep the public at a safe distance from him.

The Tasmanian government, finding itself in a precarious position, has finally decided to take action. The Department of Natural Resources and Environment published a 27-page dossier this week titled “Neil the Seal Management Plan.”

“The purpose of this Plan is to set out a framework for managing the resident elephant seal known as Neil in Tasmania, recognising the complex challenges associated with his recurring haul out period,” the dossier states.

Neil has a dedicated task force to monitor his whereabouts, and according to the dossier, they would take a “non-intervention,” hands-off approach if he hauls out in a secluded location. They’d keep tabs on Neil from a distance, erecting signs around the area to alert the public of Neil’s presence while advising them to keep their distance. Should the public tempt fate and approach Neil, the task force can call in security personnel to keep people and the seal safe.

The second contingency plan is titled “on-site seal management,” which would be necessary if Neil comes ashore in a more public location, and has immediate access to roads and critical infrastructure that up the odds of molting-induced mayhem. One proposed management option involves “hazing,” which would essentially treat Neil like a frat pledge. The dossier doesn’t get into specifics—ostensibly there’s no paddling or eating a live goldfish involved—but highlights what it calls a “non-violent method of using deterrents and negative associations to disturb an animal, compelling them to move,” which can include “controlled visual, tactile and vocal stimuli where appropriate.”

The document also notes that Neil appears to be adapting to and thus eluding “standard management practices,” meaning that the task force needs to stay nimble in coming up with new methods to curb Neil’s taste for antics.

Tasmanian officials also propose “seal enrichment,” which they say would be used in tandem with other management options, to redirect “natural exploratory behaviors” (like engaging with infrastructure) toward decoy items “designed to withstand repeated interaction.”

Officials also say that despite their best efforts to avoid Neil-related interruptions to daily life, “significant events,” such as road closures, public safety incidents, relocation or translocation activities, or wildlife-borne diseases, are still liable to happen. During such events, members of the public are advised to contact the Marine Mammal Hotline, also known as “0427 WHALES.”

#575. Disney's 'Star Wars' is coming to Cosm domes ahead of 50th anniversary as part of multiyear film deal

On Thursday, the immersive entertainment technology company announced a new studio partnership with The Walt Disney Co. that will bring the original "Star Wars" to its domes early next year as part of a multiyear, multifilm collaboration.

The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Cosm's massive concave screens will drop film fans into a galaxy far, far away starting in March, just ahead of the Academy Award-winning film's 50th anniversary in May.

"We are thrilled to add the Disney partnership," Alexis Scalice, head of Cosm Studios, told CNBC. "We do look for those opportunities of these like anniversary and commemorative moments. We look for those opportunities to celebrate with the fans, but also find this mutually beneficial partnership between both parties."

This will be Cosm's sixth theatrical collaboration with Hollywood, having already partnered with Warner Bros. to bring "The Matrix," "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" and "It" to its locations. The company is set to launch immersive screenings of Universal's "Shrek" in December.

Each Cosm dome has stadium-style seating, with booths and tables set on each level. The dome's width fills much of the viewers' periphery, giving the sensation that they are part of the onscreen environment.

In this case, "Star Wars" will be displayed in a large rectangle in the center of the dome while the background is transformed into the iconic planets of Tatooine and Yavin IV that are featured in the film as well as the infamous Death Star. Audiences will also see elements that will make it appear like they're traveling at lightspeed and getting trapped in an intergalactic trash compactor.

Cosm is working directly with studios Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic as well as creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and the sound mixing for the unique presentation of the film.

"We look for those moments where sound, music ... listening to Darth Vader's breath for the first time ... you feel those moments differently in an 87-foot diameter dome and 12k resolution with the sound system we have," Scalice said. "And it's one of the things that with experiential cinema and our technology that we were so excited and honestly privileged that we can take these defining moments for fans and work closely with our partners that doesn't really change the authenticity of it, it just enhances it in a different manner."

The premium experience will also be paired with a themed menu. Cosm has done this with other titles, such as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," serving guests throughout the screening with house-made shepherd's pie, pretzel wands with cheese dip and a box of Bertie Bott's Every Flavour Beans.

Cosm is trying to establish itself as a destination for fandom — both for sports and for film. It has a wide variety of live event offerings, which it telecasts using proprietary cameras mounted in arenas that broadcast back to the dome, as well as its expanding library of movies.

"What I love is that we really are kind of building these Cosm communities built on fandom," Scalice said. "It's the No. 1 foundation for our business."

And Star Wars is a powerful fandom. The franchise remains one of the top-ranking pieces of intellectual property across film, television and retail annually, and Disney is gearing up for a massive celebration of its semicentennial including merchandise launches, theatrical re-releases, its biannual Star Wars Celebration convention and collaborations with other brands.

#574. Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries."

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:

"In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."

The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

#573. Alligators, pet snakes, a dog on a jet ski. Meet the animals of GTA 6.

Grand Theft Auto VI launches Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and as the game unlocks around the world, players are already sharing clips of their first encounters with the local wildlife.

Beyond the streets of Vice City, Leonida — Rockstar's fictional take on Florida — is home to more than 170 animal species according to Game Informer, from alligators (that can eat you!) and manatees to jellyfish and dogs of several breeds. That's a massive jump from the roughly 28 species in GTA 5. Some are there to spot and log in your wildlife journal, while others invite you to stop and interact — and some can even become your pets.

Here's what we know about the animals in GTA 6 so far, and what you can do when you find them.

The wildlife in Leonida gets pretty specific to Florida. There are the animals you'd probably expect, like flamingos, manatees, and alligators, plus a few that might surprise you, like green iguanas, cane toads, and rhesus macaques. Yes, Florida really does have monkeys. And if you head up to Mount Kalaga, it’s worth stopping to see what’s going on around you. One of Rockstar's screenshots shows a cougar stalking a group of deer, so mind your surroundings.

So far, people have spotted everything from armadillos, beavers, and raccoons to black bears, bobcats, and boars. There are also foxes, otters, skunks, squirrels, frogs, turtles, and snakes, plus cows, horses, cats, and dogs. And if you're the kind of person who stops to pet every dog you pass, there are already reports of Australian shepherds, Chihuahuas, Dobermans, German shepherds, Labradors, and Rottweilers.

There's plenty to look for along the water, too. Think pelicans, herons, and spoonbills, along with ducks, gulls, cormorants, cranes, and those flamingos. Eagles, pigeons, storks, and woodpeckers have also turned up. In the water itself, sightings range from crayfish, eels, and jellyfish to dolphins, sea turtles, manta rays, hammerhead sharks, and whales. If you go scuba diving off the Leonida Keys, some of the marine life even glows.

A few sightings are still up for debate. GTABase lists possums and rats, for example, while IGN left both off its list.

If you pass by an adorable cat or dog, you can pet both. Petting a cat actually gives Jason a small focus boost, and if a dog's owner gives you permission, you can give it a treat. Some gas stations sell pet treats, according to The Guardian, and you also have the option to praise or scold either animal.

You can also run into a cat while stealing a car. In one clip, Jason drives off, hears loud meowing, and suddenly has a cat lunging at him. A timed button prompt lets him fend it off, and from there, you can pull over and let the cat out or keep driving. As one user put it, "Cats Are Now Gangsters."

Apparently, dogs in Leonida like jet skis, too. One player in a post on X swam out to see how far they could get from shore and found a dog sitting on a jet ski that users can ride with. How it got out there is anybody's guess.

Back on dry land, Jason has a pet of his own. Dolores, a snake, lives at his house in the Leonida Keys, and feeding her a mouse gives him a small focus boost. So far, she's the only pet Jason can keep in the story, according to Cultured Vultures.

You can also keep track of the animals you see. Open the weapon wheel, select your binoculars, and zoom in on an animal. Then hold R1 on PlayStation or RB on Xbox to add it to your wildlife logbook. There are 62 types of birds to spot, as we covered in our GTA 6 birdwatching guide, and different breeds of cats and dogs get their own entries. Studying any 100 of the 255 entries counts toward 100 percent completion, according to PowerPyx.

There's also a zoo to visit, and you can go fishing or hunting. Rockstar North's Rob Nelson told YouTuber TGG that fishing is catch-and-release, so every fish goes back in the water, even during a challenge, as GameSpot reported.

Hunting is a way to earn money. Jason's old Army friend Bret Vogel teaches him how to track deer before sending him after other animals. Some hunting challenges spell out exactly what to look for. According to the outlet, some send players after a boar, a rattlesnake, and a panther.

One challenge, the Legendary Hunter challenge, asks players to hunt eight unique animals, whose identities are still under wraps. Perhaps one of which is this unrecognizable creature. #572. France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency

Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.
