#484. Heated Rivalry 4DX is fun, but how does it compare to Wicker 4DX?

When I heard about Wicker 4DX, it seemed a cheeky joke. Praise was fervent for the fantasy romance that stars Olivia Colman as a lonely Fisherwoman who weds a Wicker Husband (Alexander Skarsgård). Admittedly, I was invested at "Olivia Colman." But buzz around the spirited sex scenes suggested Wicker 4DX would be a rollicking good time. So, naturally, as a journalist, it was my job to find out.

In my review of Wicker 4DX, I detailed how the motion-enhanced theaters "vibrated and bucked, yes, in rhythm with the Wicker Husband's thrusting." After the first love scene, the elated audience applauded and cheered. It was great fun, but also a cinematic experience that fostered a sense of community among romance fans who don't want to hide their horniness. Here was a safe space to giggle and swoon without fear of judgment. It reminded me of the gleeful days of slumber parties, and what a treasure they were.

So, my hopes were high when it was announced Heated Rivalry would follow in Wicked's bouncy footsteps.

The Canadian phenomenon went from streaming to theaters, playing two episodes at a clip for fans to rewatch together. Then, it was announced that episodes 5 and 6 would be getting the 4DX treatment. As Mashable's newly minted 4DX-pert, I was obliged to go.

So, how did Heated Rivalry 4DX compare the Wicker 4DX? Let's get into it.

I can hear you gasping. But think about it! This isn't the early days of the forbidden romance between hockey rivals Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie). What played in 4DX were the episodes "I'll Believe in Anything" and "The Cottage."

This means the screening began with the awkward morning after another fumbled hook-up between Shane and Rose Landry (Sophie Nélisse). This episode is the one where they break up, and from there, where flirtations and hand-holding suggest the intimacy between Shane and Ilya is blossoming into a love neither can admit to. That is, until Ilya does say "I love you," over the phone, in a far-away tunnel in Russia (and in Russian).

Episode 5 is full of beautiful dramatic moments, including Scott Hunter (François Arnaud) celebrating his championship win by bringing his lover Kip (Robbie G.K.) onto the ice, and coming out publicly. But there aren't many lusty moments. So, the 4DX seats would tease the audience by thrumming in sync with the show's soundtrack or vibrating anytime a text message arrived.

Episode 6 finally offers some fooling around in Shane's bedroom and then the oral sex scene, where Ilya goes down on Shane as he takes a call from Hayden (Callan Potter). Fans hooted and laughed as the seats attempted to match the rhythm of Ilya's motions. But it doesn't compare to the rocking of Wicker, which offered multiple sex scenes. The first of them is on the wedding night between the Fisherwoman and the Wicker Husband, and the motion added was so thoughtfully rendered in seat-rocking that the audience cheered upon its climax.

Heated Rivalry 4DX cannot compete here, or rather, it doesn't, by focusing on the final two episodes.

Well, for one thing, the violence hits harder. After the funeral for Ilya's father, he gets into a physical confrontation with his brother Alexei (Slavic Rogozine), who thrusts the hockey star into a wall. Ilya responds in kind, and the audience gasped as our bodies were collectively slammed in the comfort of our seats.

Likewise, the brief hockey scenes has a fresh sense of immersion. In slo-mo scenes, the seats slowly but smoothly rocked from side to side, mimicking the motion of the players' hips as they skated. And as "I'll Believe in Anything" is the episode where Shane "gets [his] bell rung," that hit is hard. But not so hard you'll get a concussion.

Of course, 4DX is more than just shimmying seats. Some charming elements included fog emitting from the front of the theater while Shane grills (too many) burgers at the cottage. Or, when Ilya is playing in the hotel pool with children or splashing in the lake near the cottage, a spritz of water was emitted. The aim seemed to be off for me and my guest, as we could see the water rise and hiss of the propulsion, but we never actually got wet, or even misted. A mist opportunity, then?

And speaking of missed opportunities, I was actually disappointed that 4DX didn't use snow.

It's an element that I saw in Wicker 4DX and was quite awed by. And it might have been mindfully employed in the tunnel scene, as snow falls in the distance as Ilya pours his heart out over the phone. In this scene, 4DX did offer a slight breeze, which was a little chilly and did enhance the experience, making it feel more like we were out in the night with this lonely lover. But snow would have been a marvelous touch.

That's not something I thought I'd ever write. But here we are.

In Wicker, I was wowed by the smell of a wet forest and of fire catching. In Heated Rivalry, I could smell the chlorine of the pool in the aforementioned hotel scene and the scent of an ice rink in the arena sequences. I could hear the hiss of the machine that emits odor throughout the two episodes. But whether it was a beach scene, the burger grilling scene, or lakeside, I couldn't smell anything but a vaguely chemical smell.

I even thought perhaps own nose was the issue, perhaps stuffy from the radical weather changes that have been hitting New York City. My sniff test was putting my bottled ice tea under my nose, but I could make out the earthy smell of the tea and the hint of lemon, and even the whiff of my perfume as my wrist raised near my nose. So, not human error!

For the sake of science, I did attend the exact same 4DX theater as I did for Wicker, though this time my seats were in the last row instead of near the front. This shouldn't have impacted the smells or splashing though. And it did have one major drawback.

Online fans of this series have ranged from enthusiastic to feral. In person, it's similarly a mixed bag. Walking into the theater, I immediately clocked fans wearing Heated Rivalry merch, like T-shirts with Shane and/or Ilya on them, jerseys with the fictional hockey teams logos, and a ball cap embroidered with "I'm coming to the cottage."

Like with Wicker DX, the energy was joyful and excited. People chatted and snacked. And I was surprised that the theater was not totally packed. But as the trailers started, more people came in. The seats slowly filled, some with fans loaded down with snacks. I will admit, my earlier 4DX experience informed our behavior here. My guest and I did buy snacks: chicken tenders, fries, and hot dogs with drinks. But we also got to the theater early enough to eat before the 4DX of it all kicked off. I'd remembered it being tricky to even eat popcorn in Wicker 4DX, in part because I'd not seen the movie before and so could not predict when my seat might buck.

Shout-out to the poor fellow to my left. He sat down during the trailers, unaware that some trailers have motion-activated moments in 4DX. As our seats bobbed up and down unexpectedly during a trailer for Disney's Hexed, I heard him gasp. I turned just in time to see the nachos leap up from their cardboard tray and into the open bag on his lap. "Oh, come on!" he yelped in righteous dismay. He was a gentleman, and tended to this snack-tastrophe as quietly as could be expected. So, this is less a scolding and more a warning: Choose your snacks and timing wisely in 4DX.

The others around me were far less mindful of others. Two women to our right talked the whole time, as if they were watching at home. Yes, they even chattered while Shane maps out their whole could-be life together in bed at the cottage. Then there was the gaggle of women who collectively left together (presumably to re-snack or use the bathroom) and made a ruckus as they went, and then used flashlights when they got back to locate something misplaced in the shuffle. Lastly, there was the woman in front of me, who kept recording the screen with her phone.

Look, I'm no fan of using phones in a theater. For one, it's a place of immersion, where we are meant to shut out the outside world. For another, it's a place of community. However slick you think you're being, you absolutely are disturbing those around you when you pull out a device that is essentially a beam of light in a dark room.

But hey, I realize 4DX is a less serious cinematic experience. It's basically movie meets ride. And so I did expect to see some phones pop up for bits of the screening, as I'd seen plenty of POV videos from Wicker 4DX's run. However, this Heated Rivalry fan was recording her clips and then logging into Instagram to post immediately after. Plus, her brightness was SO high that I could tell you her name, or at least her Insta handle.

Behavior like this disrupts other people's immersion into what they paid to see. While the recorder might be looking to build online community (or cachet) through the clips, they're essentially ignoring those around them in favor of this aim. It's sacrificing not only the recorder's ability to live in the moment of the movie (or show) but also others, without their okay.

Still, despite these anti-social choices, there were moments of glorious fan unity in Heated Rivalry 4DX. When Wolf Parade's song "I'll Believe in Anything" began to play, there was a frisson in the air that had nothing to do with pipes, odors, or shaking seats. The theater was silent as we all watched and pined for the happy ending we know by heart by now. As Kip took to the ice, I could hear choked gasps of anticipation. When Scott kisses him, there were cheers and applause. Then, when Ilya says the line ("I'm coming to the cottage"), the audience roared with excitement as if we'd won the Stanley Cup. Plus, they were chirps and cheers throughout the final sequence of episode 6, where Shane comes out to his parents and Ilya uses the word "boyfriend" for the first time.

In those moments, it was a pleasure to be in that crowd. And yet, it was easier to enjoy Wicker.

I can't be certain, but I could guess based on release dates that fewer people in the Wicker 4DX had seen the production before their showtime than was true of Heated Rivalry. The most ardent loons I know have seen the Crave series top to bottom five or six times. And perhaps that means that rather than coming for a whole experience, these 4DX attendees were coming for big emotional moments. Those don't really translate into big physical motions.

While this is a streaming drama series that does a lot of things beautifully, it's stretches of earnest dialogue don't make for the kind of unserious fun the romantic comedy of Wicker allowed for. Still, it was a fun night out to relish in a show I love with friends and fellow fans.

My advice to you, should more showtimes be added, would be if you go to Heated Rivalry 4DX, zip your lip and put your phone away. And look, if you do plan to pull out your phone, at least have enough consideration for your fellow audience member to do it with the brightness down, and maybe not smack dab in the middle of the theater. Don't make your short attention span or craving for content cachet someone else's problem.

#483. Gig Work Is Invading Nursing Homes. The Risks Can Be Deadly

Within hours of being injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center.

This investigation was produced in partnership with Proof News, a nonprofit newsroom covering AI.

Felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived. She was a gig worker who picked up her shift on the nursing app ShiftKey. She wasn’t familiar with Lewis or her roommate and never received orientation on any of the facility’s policies and procedures.

“It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August. Kaye declined to comment for this story.

Gig workers are flooding America’s understaffed nursing homes, resulting in a revolving door of staff caring for the nation’s elderly and infirm. ShiftKey boasts a network of more than 10,000 facilities—many of them nursing homes—and more than 200,000 health care workers hoping to fill shifts.

An investigation by Proof News and WIRED found that the gig nursing model is putting lives at risk: Numerous court filings, federal inspection reports, and interviews with former employees of the company, attorneys, and gig nurses themselves describe how ShiftKey thrusts workers into understaffed nursing homes with little to no onboarding—leading to dangerous situations.

In January, a federal surveyor from the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services noted that a ShiftKey worker made a mistake inserting a PICC line, a catheter threaded in a patient's arm to their heart. No one at the nursing home had checked that they were trained on the procedure. In 2025, a CMS surveyor wrote that a Texas nursing home didn’t orient temporary workers on how to feed residents before a ShiftKey worker tried to force feed one with a syringe. Later that year, a nursing home in Texas banned a ShiftKey worker after a resident who was supposed to be under her care was found sitting in urine and feces.

Inspection reports also reveal alleged abuse and theft. This summer at Hillsboro Rehab in Illinois, a ShiftKey worker allegedly stole the debit cards of two residents and used one of them at a local smoke shop and ice cream store.

According to the inspection report, the nursing home notified ShiftKey about the incident and blocked the worker in the app so they couldn’t pick up shifts there in the future. The worker was later arrested, and residents repaid, according to Tim Blythe, regional vice president of operations for Tutera, Hillsboro Rehab’s parent company.

“We sincerely regret this unfortunate incident,” Blythe wrote in an email. “We completed an internal investigation and notified the individual's employer, law enforcement, the Office of Inspector General, and appropriate regulatory agencies.”

One ShiftKey worker was accused of slapping a resident in the face in Texas in 2022, and another of “verbal abuse” of a resident in Tennessee in 2023. At the Center at Grande in Texas, a third was accused of stealing hundreds of dollars from four residents in February 2025. None of the facilities responded to a request for comment.

ShiftKey pitches itself as the Uber for nursing. “We applied technology to the nurse staffing industry,” reads an internal “selling points” memo obtained by Proof and WIRED. “What Uber did was connect the customer directly with drivers. ShiftKey connects facilities directly with providers.”

“Our technology is part of the solution to [the] patient care crisis by allowing highly experienced nurses to work on the schedules they choose and by enabling healthcare facilities to quickly fill care gaps and deliver patient care,” ShiftKey CEO Mike Vitek said in a statement to Proof News and WIRED.

Though ShiftKey advertises open shifts for a variety of facilities—including those for addiction treatment, psychiatric hospitals, and correctional institutions —a Proof News and WIRED analysis of 108,706 available shifts collected in March, July, and August 2026 found that 89 percent of open shifts were at nursing homes.

The app offers shifts for mostly lower-paid nursing staff. A majority of the open shifts Proof New and WIRED reviewed called for licensed practical nurses or certified nursing assistants, careers that don’t require a bachelor’s degree and are paid between $20 and $30 an hour on average, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

In his statement, Vitek disputed that the model is “harmful to the industry” given “long-standing, systemic issues within the healthcare ecosystem.” He emphasized that ShiftKey verifies credentials, conducts background checks, checks abuse registries, and makes that information available to facilities.

“Importantly, training or orientation required by any facility to operate within its policies is conducted by that individual facility,” Vitek said. “At ShiftKey, we do not employ nurses—we simply enable their access to flexible shifts.”

Like a growing number of platforms built to automate workforce management, ShiftKey relies on a variety of automation tools. The software allows facilities the option to automatically post and accept shifts; the app uses a “formula-based calculation” to assign workers a “reliability score,” according to Vitek, which nurses said affects their ability to get shifts; and it offers shift scoring, last-minute pricing, and dynamic pricing based on demand and supply, according to the company’s job postings and employees’ professional profiles.

After the insulin incident, Kaye testified, she wasn’t prevented from working on the platform.

In court filings, both ShiftKey and Peachtree maintain they shouldn’t be held responsible for Lewis’ death. ShiftKey argued that it is not liable because Kaye “has never been its employee,” while Peachtree said it “cannot be held liable for the acts of an independent contractor.” Kaye is not named as a defendant, and ShiftKey is paying $40,000 to settle with Lewis’ family.

A representative for Peachtree Centre declined to comment citing pending litigation. In court, the home pointed out Lewis was admitted to the hospital with many conditions besides effects from the injection, and her death certificate lists “senile degeneration of the brain” as the cause.

As part of the case, Kaye testified that she drove more than 250 miles from Myrtle Beach to work the Peachtree overnight shift. She had over two years of experience at the time and said she wasn’t given so much as a tour before being the only nurse posted to oversee a floor of 22 patients.

“This particular shift I had a lot of patients,” she testified in the August deposition. “It was very overwhelming.”

In their complaint against Peachtree and ShiftKey, Lewis’ family said they’d entrusted their “vulnerable” mother to a home they expected to “properly train staff.”

“I’ll never get Mom back,” said Lewis’ son, James Lewis, in a deposition earlier this year. “I just don't want it to happen to anybody else.”

Kara Smith can’t tell you where she’ll be working next week. A certified nursing assistant, Smith logs into the ShiftKey app most mornings to browse eight-hour shifts at more than a dozen long-term care facilities within driving distance from her West Virginia home.

Lured by the promise of scheduling freedom and premium pay for hard-to-fill shifts, Smith became a ShiftKey contractor in 2022. She claims she soon learned it's not unheard of to work night shifts at nursing homes staffed entirely by ShiftKey.

Founded in 2016 in Texas, ShiftKey grew rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, as unprepared nursing homes reeled from rolling outbreaks that could claim dozens of lives in a single facility. Health care workers sought higher pay as their risks mounted, and homes scrambled to fill shifts.

Backed by private equity, ShiftKey and its competitors Clipboard Health and IntelyCare benefited. According to an analysis by the US Department of Health and Human Services, from 2019 to 2022, the use of contract staff in nursing homes tripled from 4 to 12 percent of all nursing hours. Though it’s since declined, the rate remains higher than prepandemic.

In 2023, ShiftKey’s then CEO told Axios that the company was valued at more than $2 billion.

Nursing homes pay ShiftKey set rates for workers. The platform then “mathematically” calculates a “suggested” rate for each shift posted, Vitek said in a statement, emphasizing that dynamic pricing tools are only used to increase pay for “difficult-to-fill” shifts—and never to decrease rates.

Workers then bid to claim it. This bidding system is what got Smith hooked: Instead of accepting whatever wage a facility would offer, Smith haggled for higher pay.

“If I can even make 25 extra cents, I'm going to try to push for that,” said Smith, a 47-year-old single mom. “Every penny counts.”

Since the pandemic, however, wages on ShiftKey have plummeted, according to several nurses who spoke with Proof News and WIRED. Teresa, an LPN who declined to give her last name, joined ShiftKey in 2019. She stopped using the platform last year when she noticed competition for shifts growing—and pay rates declining.

“People were fighting over trash shifts for under $20 an hour,” said Teresa, a single mother of three kids.

Smith remembers being able to bid $3 to $4 more an hour above the facility’s suggested rate when she first joined, but this year she said she’s been forced to accept less money or risk no work at all.

According to her ShiftKey payment records that she shared with Proof News and Wired, one facility paid her $32.50 an hour in the summer of 2025 and around $26 a year later. Payments from another nursing home showed the same downward trend. On Facebook groups, many ShiftKey workers have posted about a similar dip in earnings.

“The starting bids are shamefully low,” said Smith. “It’s not worth the workload or the drive.”

During her four years with ShiftKey, Smith said she routinely felt “thrown in” at new facilities without orientation, clear instructions, or logins. She said she had to work hard to familiarize herself with the residents’ conditions, because critical details, such as who is a fall risk or who has a catheter or an ostomy, are frequently missing. Hours in, she felt like she was in “an ocean and nobody’s around me.”

“We're coming there because they're short-handed,” said Smith. “So we are automatically going to be walking into a shit show.”

Smith said a lack of orientation led to scary close calls. Last year, she says she arrived at a Virginia nursing home with no advance information, not even the door code. She didn’t know anything about the patients, and that made her “very stressed out.”

“I know my blood pressure went up because of it,” she said.

Another time, Smith said she dropped off a regular drink to a resident only to later learn that they were prescribed only thickened liquids to avoid choking.

“What if they choked and died?” said Smith.

Facilities on ShiftKey have the option to require that workers attend a paid “orientation shift” before picking up a regular one. But four ShiftKey workers told Proof News and WIRED that they've frequently picked up nursing home shifts without doing an orientation shift first.

Inspection reports from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services dating back to 2023 and obtained by Proof News and WIRED reveal ShiftKey workers making dangerous mistakes.

In Ohio, after a ShiftKey nurse made a PICC line mistake at Stellar Care Center, a federal inspection report noted that the nursing home’s administrators had never checked to see whether she was trained to do IV therapy.

The report noted that an administrator had spoken with someone at ShiftKey, who told her that because they consider everyone on the app an independent contractor, the company didn’t test for what skills they knew.

In other cases, the orientation was inadequate. At Woodway Rehabilitation and Healthcare Center in Texas, a federal health surveyor spotted a ShiftKey worker trying to force-feed a resident a health shake using an oral syringe. The ShiftKey worker said it was her first time at the facility, according to the 2025 inspection report. She received some orientation for the facility on the app before she started her shift, the report said, but couldn’t remember if feeding was included.

In 2024, another CMS surveyor wrote that a ShiftKey nurse at the Medical Suites at Oak Creek in Wisconsin told the surveyor she was not shown any care plans for residents on her first day. According to the report, the surveyor spoke with an administrator, who handed the surveyor an undated orientation checklist. The administrator said they did not currently have a policy regarding orientation for gig nurses, but that she'd be implementing one in 30 minutes.

Neither Stellar Care, Woodway Rehab, nor the Medical Suites at Oak Creek responded to requests for comment on this story.

Researchers warn that gig nurses who aren’t properly oriented and who move constantly between facilities can disrupt the continuity of care. Jasmine Travers Altizer, an assistant professor at New York University’s Rory Meyers College of Nursing, conducted a qualitative study of 22 nursing home administrators this year and found that they felt relying on temporary workers led to “less consistent care, more hospital transfers, potentially unnecessary treatments and antibiotic use, and increased falls.” Administrators also reported staff having less ability to support one another across the facility.

Gig nursing “shouldn't be a fix for chronic understaffing,” said Travers Altizer in an email. It's critical, she said, to “have consistent staff who know the residents.”

In response, Vitek, the ShiftKey CEO, said, “Continuity of care is an important consideration in nursing home quality, but the issue predates platforms like ours.”

ShiftKey says its model keeps more nurses on the job during a time of critical shortage. Vitek said a survey of workers on ShiftKey found that more than a third stated they would not be able to stay in the health care industry without such a platform.

“We reject the premise that enabling independent flexible nursing support is harmful to the industry, because the challenge in addressing these issues is not about the choice between full-time staff versus temporary shift support,” he said.

Katie Wells, a researcher who tracks gig nursing, said a combination of factors made platforms like ShiftKey an attractive option for nursing homes. Health care facilities were struggling financially, and many of them had been taken over by private equity, which Wells said “contributed to lean staffing models that make facilities more likely to want to just plug the hole rather than invest in a larger staff.”

According to CMS data, the average time worked by nursing staff per resident at Peachtree, where Lewis was accidentally injected, is lower than the state average and less than minimum requirements set by the US Department of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration that are no longer in effect. The American Health Care Association, a nonprofit group that represents nursing homes, successfully challenged the rule in court in 2025, and the Trump administration ultimately withdrew the rule, stating that the move would save nursing homes $55.1 billion over the course of 10 years.

“We need to have minimum safe staffing levels,” said Hannah Garden-Monheit, who worked on nursing home reform at the White House National Economic Council and now is executive director of Columbia Law School’s Center for Law and the Economy. “The patients need that continuity of care.”

Half a dozen ShiftKey nurses and the two former corporate employees told Proof News and WIRED that many of the facilities that use ShiftKey have a history of poor quality of care and staffing issues.

One ShiftKey nurse recalled rats scurrying in the ceiling and roaches falling from lights at one nursing home.

Constance Hicks, a longtime certified nursing assistant in Connecticut, said that most nursing homes she worked at through ShiftKey were in terrible condition: no barrier cream, no soap, no supplies. Some places had no hot water. Not once in more than a year of picking up shifts through ShiftKey does she remember receiving any training at the homes.

In November 2023, while working a double shift at Cobalt Lodge Healthcare, Hicks discovered an elderly patient with their head and neck trapped in a bed rail, their forehead compressed against the metal, according to court records. She checked the patient’s vitals and, finding dangerously high blood pressure, called 911. Even though her shift had ended, Hicks stayed until emergency workers arrived.

Hicks said she documented everything and sent it to ShiftKey. She also tried reaching out to the company’s representatives but said no one responded. By the next day, her ShiftKey account was deactivated.

Hicks, who says the incident with the patient caused “a whole lot of psychological trauma,” tried to file a lawsuit against ShiftKey over the deactivation and other issues, but court records show the company successfully moved her case to private arbitration.

Cobalt Lodge Healthcare did not respond to a request for comment, and ShiftKey declined, citing ongoing litigation.

Regarding the quality of the facilities, Vitek said, “When professionals raise a concern, we encourage them to use the formal reporting channels, and remind them that they can choose whether they can accept future shifts there.”

Some lawmakers have begun scrutinizing platforms like ShiftKey, in part over concerns that it’s misclassifying its workers as independent contractors.

“It's not like they're coming in, bringing their own tools, fixing a pipe, and leaving,” says Emma Greenman, a Minnesota state representative, of gig nurses. “They are being managed by somebody.”

ShiftKey disputes that characterization. “ShiftKey, as a technology marketplace, does not employ healthcare professionals but connects them with healthcare facilities that have gaps in their schedule,” said Vitek, adding that the company works “tirelessly” to ensure its model complies with the law.

Greenman is working on a bill that she said would curb worker misclassification in Minnesota, including in gig nursing.

“What they’re doing is building business models to evade, break, and distort labor law for profit,” Greenman said.

There’s also the issue of whether to allow nursing homes to staff largely with gig workers. The year Lewis died, an analysis of staffing data submitted to CMS shows that nearly a third of the total nursing staff hours at Peachtree were performed by temporary workers.

Gary Poliakoff, one of the attorneys representing Lewis’ family, said that some weeks, the rate of temp workers including ShiftKey rose to as high as 50 percent of all nursing staff.

With little orientation, Poliakoff said, the model puts both patients—and workers—at a “great disadvantage.”

After the mistaken insulin injection, James Lewis said he got the call from Peachtree letting him know his mother was in the hospital. According to his deposition, he was getting ready to go to church to preach and planned to visit her later. He often went every day. They’d eat lunch together and watch The Price Is Right, but that day he was looking forward to spending some time outside. It was Mother’s Day.

When asked if he knew that Peachtree sometimes had temporary workers, he responded that he wasn’t aware.

“I don't know if it was a traveling nurse or what,” he said in the deposition. “But I know it wasn't a regular person.”

In her testimony, Kaye blamed understaffing for her insulin mix-up. She remembered working at Peachtree twice in November 2021 but went six months without returning because she thought it was a “shithole.”

“It was not a nice facility by any means,” Kaye said.

She testified she was already an hour late giving the insulin, having too much on her plate.

“I remember being not helped at all by administration, not knowing who anyone was,” said Kaye. “And pretty much being by myself.”

#480. Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years

Nike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.

The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.

Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.

The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth."

Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the new initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve."

"What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill said.

He added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also said Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China.

Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.

Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.

Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.

Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.

The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.

Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.

At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.

Nike COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy told CNBC the company sees an opportunity to triple its business in the country over the next five years.

He added that Nike's broader strategy will position it for success in India.

"If you look at the three components, brand building, landing those innovations into marketplaces in an increasingly locally connected fashion and then doing all of those things in a much faster pace really aligns well with the aspirations for India," he said.

CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally.

The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

#477. 14 Best Gifts for Travelers Who Have Everything (2026)

The best gifts for travelers deliver ease and peace of mind. Even the most seasoned globe-trotter likely finds the trek stressful. Between panic-packing, navigating cramped terminals, and living out of a suitcase, being away from home can be overstimulating.

Jet-setters may think they have their travel routine down to a science, but the perfect gift can enhance any experience, whether it's a three-day business retreat or a two-week adventure across Europe. Below, find my favorite gifts for frequent travelers, from an essential suitcase set and a portable e-reader to comfortable compression socks and the perfect neck pillow.

For more travel gifts, check out our guides to the Best Travel Totes, the Best Toiletry Bags, and the Best Carry-On Suitcases.

Updated November 2026: I’ve refined our picks and added the Therabody Depuffing Wand. Prices and links were also updated.

Therabody's TheraFace Depuffing Wand doesn’t leave my side during travel. It combines hot and cold therapy to tackle puffiness, improve circulation, and better absorb skin-care products before application. The curved applicator and precision tip zero in on tricky spots, like under the eyes or across the jawline. The Depuffing Wand has three preset temperature levels for each mode. The cryotherapy is consistent throughout the six-minute session—plus, it won’t drip or crack if you forget about it in the freezer like traditional ice rollers. (Don’t put it in the freezer.) There’s also a little light that flashes at the three-minute mark to remind you to switch sides.

Every traveler needs a luggage set that includes a checked case and a carry-on. Chances are, the jet-setter in your life already has one they love. But if they’re due for a refresh, this set from Quince is an excellent (and expandable) gift. The brand makes some of my favorite travel gear, with pieces that look remarkably similar to designs from premium brands—but at a fraction of the price. This set comes in a range of minimalist colors and has all the features you could want in luggage, including 360-degree spinner wheels, a TSA-approved lock, and high-quality zippers.

For the bookworm who’s always traveling, the Kindle Paperwhite is the obvious gift. Reviewer Nena Farrell says the 12th-generation model has the highest contrast ratio of any Kindle and lasts up to three months on a single charge. Whether you're reading in direct sun or a dim plane cabin, its 7-inch display is crisp and easy on the eyes thanks to its warm backlighting. Plus, its IPX8 waterproofing rating means you can confidently read poolside without worrying about water damage. The Signature Edition adds wireless charging, auto-brightness, and double the storage at 32 GB.

Check out our guides to the Best Kindles and the Best E-Readers for more recommendations.

If you’re traveling abroad—or just don’t yet have your Real ID—a travel wallet is a must. The puffy Luka from Calpak comes in 23 colors, so you’re sure to find an option that fits your giftee’s vibe. It’s got plenty of room for cash, cards, your passport, and other documents, and it zips securely for peace of mind. Just note that it is quite large—about the size of a mass-market paperback. On the plus side, this makes it easy to find at a glance in a big bag or backpack. On the minus, a flight attendant once asked me to put it in the overhead compartment when she saw it on my lap. —Kat Merck

Check out our guide to the Best Packing Cubes for more recommendations.

Do you know a frequent traveler who’s always headed somewhere sunny and always comes back with a sunburn as a souvenir? Solbari’s hats make the perfect gift, as they're all designed for sun protection with built-in Ultraviolet Protection Factor (UPF). As a resident of sunny San Diego, I wear this UPF 50+ hat often to protect my face and scalp, but it would work well anywhere. It travels well, too, since it’s soft, flexible, and doesn't take up much space. I regularly stow it in the bottom of my beach bag or stroller, and it would also be easy to pack in a carry-on. —Nena Farrell

This is my all-time favorite travel makeup bag. It comes in eight colors and three sizes (small, medium, and large). The medium has enough room for all the makeup I need for a two-week trip, and I'm an overpacker. It has 15 small pockets in addition to four larger mesh pockets, three flexible compartments, and two adjustable dividers, meaning you'll have a designated spot for nearly every product you own, including your makeup brushes. The customizable layout lets you configure it around what you actually pack. And it also feels and looks luxe. For everyday needs, get the small. The medium is my pick for short trips, and the large has enough space to double as a toiletry bag for longer trips.

Airports are chaotic enough without needing to worry about losing your luggage. AirTags can be a bit divisive, but they’re the best way to keep tabs on your valuables if you have an iPhone. Plus, with busy flights often leading to last-minute gate checks and delays, AirTags are well worth the extra security. If your friend or loved one is an Android user, I recommend the Chipolo Pop instead.

Check out our guide to the Best Bluetooth Trackers for more recommendations.

Traveling means sacrificing the comfort of your bed and sometimes facing unpredictable sleeping conditions. An eye mask for sleep is a small luxury that can make even the least ideal sleep arrangements more tolerable. I love Bearaby's full temple-to-temple coverage and gentle fit that doesn't squeeze your head. Made from natural eucalyptus fibers, it's breathable and anti-frizz, which is perfect for anyone who styles their hair before flights.

Check out our guide to the Best Sleep Masks for more recommendations.

If I’m traveling away from home, whether for a day or a week, it’s a sure bet that I have Rumpl’s machine-washable Travel Puffy with me. I’ve had to use it for countless unexpected situations—sitting on something cold or wet, napping or relaxing at the airport or on a cold airplane, using it as a beach or picnic blanket, or just wearing it as a poncho because I forgot a jacket. (It has a little clip in the front for this purpose.) #476. Scientists found a star inside of another giant star

Astronomers have detected a star slightly less massive than the sun inside a giant star for the first time.

The two stars, in the nearby Andromeda Galaxy, had circled each other for thousands of years. Then the giant swallowed the smaller star. The trapped star took only about seven years to spiral to the center, where the two merged into a single star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope supplied the final evidence.

Scientists think the same kind of spiral explains how many star pairs end up circling each other very closely. In this case, the small star didn't survive. But in other pairs, the giant's gas gets blasted away first, leaving both stars in an orbit that takes just hours or days instead of years. Those tight pairs can later become black holes or super-dense dead star cores called neutron stars, or explode as supernovas. Some also send out gravitational waves, which are ripples in space and time.

Lead author Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University, and an international team reported the discovery Wednesday in the journal Nature.

The researchers nicknamed the larger star "Big Bao," and it earned the name. It had about seven times the sun's mass and 350 times its width, shining 18,000 times brighter.

"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said Karel Temmink, a doctoral student at Radboud University in the Netherlands, in a statement.

Its partner, "Little Bao," had about 70 percent of the sun's mass.

Stars like Big Bao swell up near the end of their lives. If our sun did the same, it could grow past Earth's orbit. As Big Bao swelled, Little Bao began skimming its outer layer and stripping away gas. Soon the small star was orbiting inside the giant. The gas there was spread so thin that Little Bao stayed intact for years, according to the paper. Still, the gas slowed it down, much like air slows a thrown ball, until it eventually sank toward the giant's core.

No telescope can literally see inside a star. But friction from the small star's plunge churned the giant's gas and carried that heat to the surface. There it showed up as seven years of steady brightening. When the team compared the starlight from before and after the eruption — and tested computer models against it — the best explanation was a small star spiraling inside the giant.

When the smaller one finally reached the giant core, gravity likely ripped it apart. That triggered a blast that hurled about one-tenth of the giant's outer material into space.

Their encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," said Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia.

Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable's Top Stories newsletter today.

The explosion itself came on surprisingly fast. The team thought an outburst would take years. Instead, it took just a week from when its brightness started rising to its peak, said Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain.

Scientists expect many star pairs to go through this phase, but catching one in the act has taken incredible luck.

"The timescales involved are short, months to years, and the rates at which they form are low," astrophysicist Jason Nordhaus wrote in a commentary published alongside the study. "Just a few stars exist in this phase at any given time in a galaxy such as the Milky Way."

Astronomers usually piece together star mergers long after they happen. This time, a fleet of telescopes followed Bao as the events unfolded. The team first noticed the star acting strangely in Feb. 2023, in data from NASA's now-retired NEOWISE mission. In Sep. 2024, another telescope saw it brightening and puffing out dust. In July 2025, NASA's Spherex telescope happened to catch it fading in visible light while it brightened in infrared light. Then, on Oct. 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility, a sky-scanning telescope in California, spotted the eruption.

Webb took its look on Dec. 24, 2025, just 47 days after the eruption peaked. No telescope had ever followed up on an event like this so quickly, Karambelkar said.

What the newly single star, now just called "Bao," will become remains an open question. Only future observations will show how it settles down.

NASA's new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile will scan huge areas of sky over and over. They should spot events like this in hundreds of nearby galaxies.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar said.

#474. These are the 3 best headphones under $300 I tested in 2026

The best headphones shouldn't be the ones that bring on credit card debt. As a professional headphone reviewer, I'm partial to a pair of well-executed flagship headphones, but I don't always find the $450 price point practical for most folks — especially when you can often find headphones for literally hundreds of dollars cheaper that perform 80 percent as well.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Especially as we head into the holiday season and Black Friday deals heat up, it can be tempting to grab the $450 flagship headphones on sale. And yes, I always recommend squeezing all the value you can, but great sales also mean mid-range headphones that are already under the $300 mark at full price are not only likely to drop to $200 or less — they already have. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

With that in mind, I rounded up my three favorite pairs of headphones under $300 that I tested in 2026. I also included one bonus option in honor of the holiday sale season.

Check out our full review of the Sony XM4C headphones.

Anyone looking for the best blend of sound, comfort, and price: Sony brought back its viral XM4 headphones with the second-generation XM4Cs. The design remains unchanged from the first generation, but sound gets a boost, making them the best-sounding headphones under $300 I've tried, and a no-brainer for students, office workers, or anyone looking to get as close as possible to the flagship headphone experience, minus the price.

Plenty of $450 headphones don't feature 10-band equalizers. Sony's WH-1000XM4C headphones do. That said, even if you don't like to mess around with a companion app, these headphones sound balanced and rich out of the box, making everything from classical piano concertos to classic rock shine. While their sound quality is certainly a huge draw, it's far from the only standout feature of these headphones.

Sony struck simplistic gold with the design of the XM4 headphones in 2020 — which is why some fans were sad to see the iconic look go in the XM5 and XM6 headphones. Now, prospective buyers don't have to decide between the latest tech and the coveted XM4 design. While Sony didn't add any improvements to the ANC (it still features the same four mics and QN1 processor it did in 2020), the internals of the sound quality make these a much easier (and easier to get) recommendation in 2026. Like the OG XM4s, these headphones also are relatively low profile, with plenty of cushioning in the headband and ear cups, minus any overbearing squeeze. The result is solid passive noise cancellation, with comfort enough to get you through a work or school day's worth of wear.

The biggest cons of these headphones are that they lack spatial audio and the battery life got bumped down three hours from the first to the second gen — 30 to 27 hours. However, the 27-hour range still sits above other (more expensive) mid-range options, so it's not the most devastating loss. And at full price, they're still less than half the price of Sony's other 2026 release: the ultra-premium 1000X the Collexion headphones.

Check out our full review of the Nothing Headphone (a).

People who like their headphones to make a statement: The Nothing Headphone (a) are going to turn some heads. The rectangular ear cup and semi-transparent design meld together the past and the future in a way that is unmistakably Nothing. Don't get me wrong, though; they don't just look good. These headphones pack a relatively balanced soundscape and decent ANC.

They're also the perfect headphones for anyone who isn't too great about plugging their devices in regularly, as they pack a whopping 75 hours of listening time per charge, with the ANC on.

These are the best headphones Nothing makes, thanks to their combo of performance and value, and the value prop here is strong. When brainstorming the best headphones under $300, the Headphone (a) immediately came to mind because they offer something most budget-oriented headphones don't (or can't, due to budget constraints): an unmistakable style. These headphones aren't trying to dupe any other one on the market.

Instead, Nothing uses the more plastic-heavy design to its advantage, securing a cool retro look, all the while offering four colorways: White, black, pink, and yellow. The power of the design doesn't stop there. The on-ear controls of these headphones are so intuitive, both in their function and placement, that I rarely reached for my device when wearing them.

Sound-wise, these aren't going to blow you away — there are likely better options for sound quality and ANC around this price point. But they get the job done, and likely won't make you regret making a decision based on aesthetics. They're a little fussy to carry around, but with headphones that look this good, I'm betting most folks will want to wear them more often than not.

On sale, these headphones have dropped as low as $109, giving them a truly impressive value prop.

Check out our full review of the Soundcore Space 2.

Bargain hunters: If you're looking for the cheapest possible option that will still offer a mid-range experience, the Soundcore Space 2 headphones are the way to go. With sound, comfort, and an overall experience that punches above its price point, I recommend these headphones to anyone looking to spend less than $200.

As nice as the XM4C headphones are, they're still an investment. These Soundcore headphones keep performance high on the core features of headphones, while showing their price point in places that don't detract too much from the overall user experience.

Let's start with how they wear. The memory foam cushions are plush, and the headphones themselves squeeze enough to offer some passive noise cancellation and stay secure, without skewing into headache-inducing territory. In other words, I could wear them for hours at a time without issue. The on-ear controls were great too, with buttons easy to find blindly and use for playback. The look isn't half bad either — at a glance, you could almost mistake them for a pair of Beats.

The sound and active noise cancellation did the job. On the former front, it came out balanced, if a bit unremarkable. Still, that's not a knock at this price point — they could sound a lot worse. ANC-wise, these feel like great daily drivers, but maybe not the satisfactory answer for anyone who has extra noisy neighbors, co-workers, or lives near a construction site. A plane ride, however? Yeah, these will do the job just fine.

My biggest warning on the sound front? Without audio playing, I could hear some minor squeaking while moving my head around, but not every single time. Not ideal, but certainly not a dealbreaker, either.

Check out our full review of the Bose QuietComfort headphones (2nd gen).

Frequent travelers, those who prioritize comfort, and anyone who happens to catch a sale: The thing about Bose is they're going to make an incredibly comfortable pair of headphones, and the second-generation QuietComforts are no exception. I wore these headphones through long work and travel days, and they felt comfortable the entire time I wore them — glasses, earrings, and all.

The only major catch? At full price, they don't fall into the under-$300 criteria. That said, I've seen them fall below that price point thanks to sales enough times that they at least deserve an honorable mention spot on this list.

Similar to the Sonys, these Bose headphones verge on the premium headphone experience. This is especially the case thanks to the balanced sound and presence of spatial audio, which narrows the gap between the $450 Bose QC Ultra headphones and these. The active noise cancellation is some of the best available, and while I dealt with some clipping on especially loud noises (think plane engines during takeoff or trains screeching up to the platform), for the most part these headphones give the cocoon of silence to expect from Bose.

I used them while flying up the west coast, and found them to be the perfect travel headphones. Though they're on the shorter side of battery life, it was still plenty to last me through my trip, and that was with heavy wear during the travel days — these headphones are comfortable enough to simply keep on. While better equalizer options would truly take these headphones over the top to more premium territory, the Bose QCs make up for it in other areas. The replaceable ear cups, for instance, mean that you can extend the life of your headphones once they start to wear down. And while the price point is on the higher side, grabbing them on sale makes them one of the best value finds in the headphones market, especially if you prioritize comfort and noise cancellation above all else.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. #472. Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence company AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, said that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions."

The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

The biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

Industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

The fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

#471. 10 Best Therabody Gadgets & Theraguns to Gift This Year (2026)

Theraguns are the gold standard for massage guns; the brand name has come to be synonymous with the entire product category, much like “Kleenex” is for tissues. But Therabody, the innovative company behind Theragun, offers more than relief for sore muscles and pain. It now sells a broad repertoire of wellness gadgets aimed at alleviating ailments like eye strain, menstrual cramps, and skin puffiness (to name a few). So whether you’re shopping for a fitness lover or someone who could use a little self-care, there’s likely a Therabody gadget worth wrapping up.

I haven't yet tried every product in the Therabody lineup (I’m getting there), but I've put most to the test and am ready to recommend my favorites. Plus, most are FSA/HSA-eligible and designed with USB-C charging capability.

Need more gift ideas for the active person in your life? Check out our guides to the Best Massage Guns, Best Massagers, and Best Compression Boots.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Theragun Prime (6th Gen) and removed discontinued products. I also confirmed up-to-date links and prices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

If you’re looking for a professional-grade massage device, the Theragun Pro Plus is one of the most advanced percussive guns on the market, incorporating vibrations, heat, and near-infrared LED therapies for an all-in-one recovery tool. It also offers cold therapy, but you'll have to purchase an additional attachment for $100 to make use of that capability—a steep add-on for what is already a splurge. After testing the attachment myself, I don't think it justifies the cost unless you are sure you'd regularly use the contrast therapy.

Priced at $650, this is the most expensive Theragun, so I'd recommend it to athletes or those who are dealing with chronic muscle pain and want the LED therapy. For casual users, some of the features might feel like overkill. For example, there's a built-in biometric sensor for heart rate tracking that I have barely used. I do, though, appreciate the OLED screen, which displays a force meter, so you can see exactly how much pressure you're applying. It's a useful function if you need a nudge to apply more pressure or a reminder to ease up.

The Theragun Prime (6th Gen) hits the sweet spot between the elite Pro Plus and the budget-friendly Relief. It’s still a premium percussive massage gun, with five speed settings, two attachments (a dampener and standard ball), and up to 120 minutes of battery life. You won’t get extras like heated or near-infrared LED therapy, or compatibility with Therabody’s cold and vibration attachments, but you will enjoy top-notch durability. It’s the only Theragun in the lineup rated to withstand drops from up to 10 feet, making it an excellent gift for the accident-prone person in your life.

The Theragun Relief, launched in 2023, remains the cheapest Theragun—priced even lower than the Mini Plus. For the price tag, you’re sacrificing some of the premium features, like the LCD screen and Bluetooth connectivity to the Therabody app for device control. But you can still follow guided routines on the app, and the simple one-button control is refreshingly simple to use.

The Relief comes with three head attachments and has three speed settings, which is a step down from models that offer a standard five speeds and four or more attachments. Still, the Relief is less than half the weight of the Pro Plus, and it's equipped with the essentials, which is more than enough for the average person.

The original Theragun Mini is still a solid portable device—and it's $60 less—but the Mini Plus feels like a shrunken version of the elite Pro Plus. The ergonomic triangular design lets me target trigger points and muscle groups like my hamstrings and calves with more pressure control (though, admittedly, that same shape makes it awkward to use on my lower back). Thoughtful details, like a travel lock to prevent it from powering on and a compact carrying pouch, make it easy to carry on commutes and flights.

Most notably, it brings heated percussive therapy to a travel-friendly device. The heat therapy is easily my favorite feature on the Pro Plus. The Mini Plus is also compatible with Therabody's Vibration Plus and Cold Plus attachments (both sold separately).

Note: Some customers have reported charging issues, saying their units wouldn't power up, but I haven't run into any battery problems in my two weeks of testing. I'll update this review if anything shifts with long-term use.

The JetBoots Pro Plus are full-length, wireless boots that combine pneumatic compression with vibration therapy and infrared LED light. Everything is controlled from a built-in LCD screen and control panel on the lead boot, and connectivity is effortless, automatically linking when powered on.

Eight preset programs target legs, knees, and joints, but you can manually adjust pressure, intensity, and the session length. Sessions can run from 10 to 60 minutes in five-minute increments, with compression adjustable between 20 and 100 millimeters of mercury (mmHg)—a standard unit of measurement for pressure. Vibration offers three intensity levels (low, medium, and high), and the infrared LED setting is a simple on or off, with an automatic shutoff after 45 minutes.

Inside the boots, a nonporous proprietary material reduces moisture and microbial buildup, and after months of testing, I haven't noticed any lingering odors. These are best suited for athletes, frequent travelers, or anyone managing circulation-related conditions. Conveniently for those aforementioned jet-setters, the JetBoots Pro Plus are TSA-approved for carry-on travel; just keep in mind that they're pretty hefty.

I enjoyed the original TheraFace Mask, but the upgraded TheraFace Mask Glo feels like the smarter purchase. It's easier to find (Therabody seems to be phasing out the original), costs $270 less, and is slightly lighter at 1.13 pounds versus the OG's 1.27 pounds. While the Glo has fewer LED bulbs—504 compared to 648—the difference doesn't translate to a lesser treatment. You get the same red, infrared, and blue light wavelengths, plus the signature vibration therapy that made the first-generation mask stand out.

The vibrations are now integrated into the adjustable straps rather than the mask itself. They're usually distracting, occasionally even headache-inducing, depending on my mood. I usually skip the vibration setting altogether to make this component less irritating. Even without it, the Glo remains competitively priced among high-end LED masks.

Treatment sessions range from four to 12 minutes, and the removable eye shields are thoughtful, but I prefer taking them off to extend the light coverage to my under-eye area. I very much appreciate the cordless design, but I do miss the display stand that came with the original. I often end up storing it back in its box, which makes me less inclined to reach for it. If you, too, deal with this issue, you might consider buying a travel case for $80.

I challenge you to stay awake through a full session with the SmartGoggles 2.0. I’ve been testing them for months, and more often than not, I conk out while wearing them. The combination of gentle heat, vibration, and massage therapy across my forehead, eyebrows, and temples relaxes my facial tension within minutes. I love wearing them when I have a headache from staring at screens all day, and while I don’t struggle with regular migraines, I can see them being a soothing blackout remedy in a quiet, dark room.

Former reviewer Medea Giordano loved the first model, and this upgrade improves the fit with contoured padding that feels similar to Therabody’s SleepMask. You still get three preset modes: Focus, Sleep, and SmartRelax. That last option uses biometric feedback to adjust vibration patterns based on your heart rate. It also syncs with the Therabody app, letting you tweak the vibration and heat intensities or incorporate sound therapy. Note, though, if you’re a side-sleeper, you’ll have to shift around, as these are most comfortable while lying flat on your back.

I’ve tested several sleep masks, and the TheraFace SleepMask is among my favorites. Many claim to be 100 percent blackout, but this one leaves me feeling totally disoriented when I wake up, with no idea what dimension I'm in—just how I like it. The contoured padding feels plush, and the adjustable strap keeps the mask in place without tugging at my hair, even when I shift around at night. It comes with a carrying case, so I always pack it for travel.

The selling point is that this mask uses vibrations—three pattern presets (Pulse, Wave, Constant)—designed to nudge your brain into deeper rest. I struggle with staying asleep, but when I wake up in the middle of the night, I just tap the button to start a 15-minute session, and it usually lulls me back to sleep. That said, the vibrations are almost too gentle; you barely feel them, but you can absolutely hear them. It's not as soothing as a white noise machine, so if you're a light sleeper, this might be a deal-breaker.

The TheraFace Depuffing Wand has become a staple in my travel bag. It delivers both hot and cold therapy to help reduce puffiness, improve circulation, and enhance product absorption before completing your skin care routine. It’s TSA-friendly—zero awkward bag checks and counting—and ideal for tackling under-eye bags after a long flight or night. The curved applicator reaches every contour of my face, and the precision tip is great for trickier spots like under my eyes. It’s intended to be used on clean, dry skin, so I hold the opposite side of my face to prevent tugging.

The wand comes with three preset temperature levels that feel gentle but effective. While the cold function isn’t as icy as a roller fresh from the freezer, it’s consistent throughout a six-minute session and doesn’t drip. Plus, this one won’t crack if you forget to take it out of the freezer (RIP to two of my traditional rollers). An indicator light flashes at three minutes to remind you to switch sides, but this notification is easy to miss if you’re not looking straight into a mirror.

Cupping is an ancient healing technique that uses suction to provide muscle relief. Therabody's version combines suction, heat, and vibration therapy for localized recovery. With three levels of suction (30, 40, and 50 kilopascals, or kPa), three heat intensities (41, 43, and 45 degrees Celsius), and three vibration modes (low, high, and wave), I appreciate how you can customize the intensity of your session. The TheraCup is also programmed with an auto-shutoff after three minutes—so you don’t overdo any area—and built-in safety sensors that will cut off the pressure if it exceeds 60 kPa.

TheraFace Mask for $650: The TheraFace Mask is a cordless, hands-free light-therapy device that uses three wavelengths (red, infrared, and blue) to tackle different skin care goals. As a distinguishing feature from its competitors, the TheraFace Mask includes a built-in vibration therapy mode that massages pressure points around the eyes, brow line, and scalp for some added stress relief. It comes with removable eye shields and a sleek display stand, which makes it easy to store on your nightstand.

JetBoots Prime for $550: Compared to the JetBoots Pro Plus, the JetBoots Prime is simple to use: You get four pressure levels (25, 50, 75, and 100 mmHg) and three durations (20, 40, or 60 minutes), all adjustable throughout your session through a built-in control panel. Th boots are wireless with a 180-minute battery life and can even be used while charging. Plus, they fold down into the included drawstring bag, making them portable and fuss-free to stow away.

WaveRoller for $180: Foam rollers are great for improving range of motion, increasing blood flow, and reducing muscle tension. You can buy a decent foam roller for significantly less, but with the WaveRoller, you get Therabody app integration for a personalized experience and five vibration frequencies. Designed for full-body use, it works best for warm-ups and post-workout recovery.

Theragun Mini (3rd Generation) for $220: I recommend the Mini if you’re new to percussive therapy or need something packable for travel. #469. Apples iPhone Duo gets Face ID, sort of

One of iPhone Duo's biggest disadvantages is the lack of Face ID. Apple's convenient way of unlocking the phone just by presenting your face simply did not fit on the thin foldable device, so Apple went with Touch ID on the power button instead.

But Touch ID, as quick as it is, is just a tad more of a hassle than simply picking the Duo up and having it unlock with a glance. Luckily, Apple figured out a way to fix this.

In the latest developer beta of iOS 27.3, the Duo has a new option, located under Settings - Touch ID & Passcode, called "Unlock with Front Camera." Turn it on, go through a quick onboarding process (similar to the one you do with the regular Face Unlock on other iPhones), and you'll be able to unlock the foldable just by looking at its front screen.

I've tried it out on my Duo, and it works as expected, easily unlocking the phone every time, even when my face was a little off to the side. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

There are caveats here, though. Face ID includes a 3D scanning mechanism making it a lot more secure, while this new feature on the Duo uses the front camera alone for face recognition. This is why Apple put a few additional safeguards in place. First, this system only works for unlocking the phone; for Apple Pay or accessing your password, you'll still need to use Touch ID. Also, face unlock won't work after 45 minutes of inactivity; you'll have to use Touch ID or passcode after that much time has passed. Finally, the system only works on the outer display, which has a better camera. Unlocking the phone via the FaceTime camera on the inner display will not work.

Apple's own warning below the option in the settings confirms this. "Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it's closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device. To use Apple Pay or to access your password, Touch ID is still required."

If you don't mind the weakened security, this is a pretty handy option, even given its limitations. I've already set up to unlock the iPhone Duo with my Apple Watch Ultra, so this doesn't change much, but users who don't have the Watch or don't wear it all the time might appreciate the face unlock feature.
